definition.text: A database index is a data structure that speeds up finding rows in a table, at the cost of extra writes and storage to maintain it.

facts.text: An index lets the database locate rows quickly without examining every row of the table, and it can be built on one or more columns, giving rapid random lookups and efficient ordered access.
An index is a copy of selected columns, like a table of contents, storing the column and a key or pointer to the whole row so the complete row can be retrieved efficiently.
Without an index, finding a row by a field value tests items one by one, which takes O(N) linear time on average; indexes give sub-linear lookup.
Many index designs give logarithmic O(log(N)) lookup, and some applications can reach flat O(1) lookup.
An index trades increased storage and slower writes, since the index must be updated along with the data, for faster reads; designs balance lookup speed, index size and update cost.
Indexes also create different views of the same data, so large data sets can offer different filters or sorting schemes without extra copies of the data.
Some databases index values transformed by a function or expression, such as upper(last_name), or build a partial index only for records meeting a condition.
Many transactions access an index at once, so it needs concurrency control; specialized index methods exist and are applied together with the usual database ones for a performance gain.

title: Clustered and non-clustered indexes
article: Database index#Index architecture and indexing methods > Clustered

definition.text: A clustered index stores a table's rows in the order of the index key, while a non-clustered index is a separate sorted structure that points to rows stored elsewhere.

facts.text: A clustered index puts the data rows on disk in the same order as the index, so a table can have only one clustered index.
Clustering helps mainly when data is read sequentially in index order or as a range, because neighbouring rows are adjacent and fewer data block reads are needed.
A non-clustered index keeps its keys in sorted order and its leaf level points to each record, so the physical row order differs from the index order.
A table can have many non-clustered indexes, usually on non-primary-key columns used in JOIN, WHERE and ORDER BY clauses.
In Microsoft SQL Server the leaf node of a clustered index is the actual data, not a pointer to data stored elsewhere as in a non-clustered index.

definition.text: In an index on several columns, the order of the columns decides which searches the index can serve.

facts.text: Row identifiers can be retrieved using only the first indexed column, but on most databases it is not possible or efficient to use only the second or a later column.
In a phone book ordered by city, then last name, then first name, listing one city's numbers is easy, but finding every entry for one last name is tedious.
With an index on (city, last_name, first_name), a search on city and first_name uses only city, then checks first_name sequentially.
To improve performance, create the index in the order of the search columns.

definition.text: A covering index is an index that itself contains all the fields a query needs, so the query is answered without reading the table record.

facts.text: Usually an index only locates the data records and the required data is read from the table; a covering index holds the needed fields itself and can answer the query.
To find the Name for ID 13, an index on (ID) still requires reading the record, but an index on (ID, Name) removes that lookup.
A covering index can speed retrieval dramatically but may be large because of the extra keys, which slow down inserts and updates.
Some systems let non-key fields be included only at the leaf level, giving a covering index with less overall size, for example with an INCLUDE clause.

title: Full table scans and index limits

definition.text: A full table scan is a query plan in which the database reads the searched column of every row because no index can be used.

facts.text: Without an index, a query on last_name must look at that column on every row, a full table scan; with an index the database follows the index structure, typically a B-tree, which is much cheaper.
A leading wildcard such as LIKE '%@wikipedia.org' cannot use the index, which assumes words go from left to right, so the database performs a full index scan; the clause is not sargable.
An extra index on reverse(email_address), queried with the reversed pattern, puts the wildcard at the right-most part of the query where the index can satisfy it.
With wildcards on both sides the index is not used and a sequential search takes O(N) time; a full-text approach such as trigrams in a GIN index lowers lookup to about O(logN).

title: Indexes and database constraints
article: Database index#Usage > Policing the database constraints

definition.text: Databases use indexes to enforce constraints such as UNIQUE, EXCLUSION, PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY.

facts.text: Declaring an index UNIQUE creates an implicit constraint on the underlying table.
Databases usually create an index implicitly on columns declared PRIMARY KEY, and some can reuse an existing index to enforce that constraint.
Many databases require both the referencing and referenced columns of a FOREIGN KEY to be indexed, which improves inserts, updates and deletes on the tables involved.
An EXCLUSION constraint ensures a predicate holds for no other record; it can implement UNIQUE or rules such as no overlapping time ranges.

definition.text: A database index can be built on several data structures, and the best choice depends on the workload.

facts.text: The index format that fits depends on whether data is indexed in memory or on disk, the data formats, and whether the system is write-heavy or read-heavy.
A skiplist is a common in-memory index type, a hash index is a common implementation of a map, and an SSTable is an immutable on-disk map.
An LSM tree combines a skiplist and SSTables for high write throughput, while a B-tree is a disk-based structure with consistent read and write performance.
An inverted index serves document indexing, a suffix tree serves string pattern search, and an R-tree serves multi-dimensional search such as finding the nearest neighbor.
Popular index implementations include balanced trees, B+ trees and hashes.

title: Bitmap index
article: Database index#Types of indexes > Bitmap index

definition.text: A bitmap index stores most of its data as bit arrays and answers queries by performing bitwise logical operations on them.

facts.text: Common indexes such as B+ trees work best when the indexed values do not repeat, or repeat only a few times.
A bitmap index is designed for values that repeat very frequently, such as a field with at most three distinct values.
For such variables a bitmap index can have a significant performance advantage over the commonly used trees.

title: Types of database indexes
article: Database index#Types of indexes > Reverse index

definition.text: Beyond the main tree and hash designs, databases use dense, sparse, reverse-key, inverted, primary and secondary indexes, among others.

facts.text: A dense index holds a key-pointer pair for every record of the sorted data file, while a sparse index holds a pair only for every block of the data file.
A reverse-key index reverses the key before entering it, for example 24538 becomes 83542, which suits sequence numbers whose new values increase monotonically.

A primary index holds the table's key fields with a pointer to the non-key fields and is created automatically with the table; a secondary index covers fields that are neither ordering nor key fields.
An inverted index maps a content word to the document containing it, which allows full-text searches.

definition.text: Database normalization is the process of structuring a relational database according to normal forms to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity.

facts.text: Normalization organizes a database's columns and tables so that their dependencies are properly enforced by integrity constraints.
It applies formal rules either by synthesis, creating a new database design, or by decomposition, improving an existing design.
Edgar F. Codd first proposed normalization as part of his relational model.
The goal is that each elementary fact is recorded in only one place, so insertions, updates and deletions automatically maintain consistency.
A fully normalized database can take new types of data with minimal changes to its structure, so applications that use it are minimally affected.
Normalization reduces data redundancy, increases data consistency, gives a better data design and enforces referential integrity.
Its costs are a more complex data design, more joins, slower performance and maintenance overhead.

definition.text: Anomalies are the undesirable side effects that can arise when modifying a relation that has not been sufficiently normalized.

facts.text: Codd's objectives for normalization included freeing relations from undesirable insertion, update and deletion dependencies and reducing the need to restructure as new data types are introduced.
Insertion anomaly: some facts cannot be recorded, such as a newly hired faculty member with no course yet, unless the Course Code is set to null.
Update anomaly: the same information on several rows means a partly applied update, such as an address changed on some skill records only, leaves the relation inconsistent.
Deletion anomaly: deleting data for one fact forces deleting a different fact, such as losing a faculty member when their last course record is removed.
Most 3NF relations are free of insertion, update and deletion anomalies.

definition.text: Normal forms are a ladder of increasingly strict rules for relations, from first normal form to sixth normal form.

facts.text: From least to most normalized the forms are UNF, 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, EKNF, BCNF, 4NF, ETNF, 5NF, DKNF and 6NF.
1NF requires scalar columns that cannot hold relations or composite values; 2NF requires every non-prime attribute to depend on the whole of every candidate key.
3NF requires every non-trivial functional dependency to begin with a superkey or end with a prime attribute; BCNF requires it to begin with a superkey.
Informally a relation is called normalized if it meets third normal form.
Normal forms beyond 4NF are mainly of academic interest because the problems they solve rarely appear in practice.

BCNF is a slightly stronger version of 3NF, sometimes called 3.5NF, that addresses anomalies 3NF as originally defined does not handle; it requires 3NF and that every functional dependency X to Y has a superkey X.

Real-world designs cannot always comply perfectly; Singh advises that if one of the first three rules is violated, the application must anticipate problems such as redundant data and inconsistent dependencies.
Codd introduced 1NF in 1970, 2NF and 3NF in 1971, and with Boyce the Boyce-Codd normal form in 1974; Fagin added 4NF in 1977 and 5NF in 1979.

definition.text: Normalization is a design technique that takes a relational table up through successive normal forms by splitting out data that violates each one.

facts.text: The process is progressive: a higher normal form cannot be reached until the previous levels are satisfied, although in practice some steps can be skipped because the data is already partly normalized.
1NF needs each field to hold a single value, so a Subject field holding a set of values is extracted into a separate Title-Subject table.
2NF needs every non-candidate-key attribute to depend on the whole candidate key; Price depended on Format as well as Title, so Price moves to its own table keyed by Title and Format.
3NF removes transitive dependencies: Author Nationality depends on Author, which depends on Title, so nationality, publisher country and genre name each move into their own tables.
4NF: if every book is offered in each location, Title is not bound to a Location, so the Franchisee-Book-Location table is split into Franchisee-Book and Franchisee-Location.
Fixing a violation of one normal form often also fixes a violation of a higher one.

title: Sixth normal form and columnar stores

definition.text: A table is in sixth normal form when each row holds the primary key and at most one other attribute.

facts.text: The drawback of 6NF is a proliferation of tables: a 5NF table with one key column and N attributes needs N tables, and multi-field updates, inserts and deletes touch several tables.
For this reason 6NF should not be used in databases serving online transaction processing (OLTP).
Data warehouses, which do not permit interactive updates, use an internal 6NF representation in some DBMSs, known as a columnar data store.
Column-oriented storage can save significant space through compression when a column has far fewer unique values than the table has rows, and it speeds up range queries.

definition.text: Locks maintain data consistency and integrity in multi-user environments by preventing simultaneous modifications that could leave data inconsistent.

facts.text: Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts will occur, so it locks the data before any change and blocks other users from accessing and updating it until the lock is released.
Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare, lets multiple users access data at once, checks for conflicts when changes are committed and rolls the operation back if one is detected.
Pessimistic locking is better for data integrity but can hurt performance; optimistic locking is better for efficiency and performance.
Good practice is to hold locks for the minimum time, lock at the most granular level such as rows rather than tables, and retry transactions that fail due to conflicts.

definition.text: The biggest difference between the two index structures is that a B-tree enables faster reads while an LSM-tree enables fast writes.

facts.text: B-tree is the most widely used indexing data structure in almost all relational databases, and its basic unit of storage is usually called a page.
Looking up a key in a B-tree traces down the range of keys until the actual value is found.
LSM-tree is widely used by NoSQL databases such as Cassandra, LevelDB and RocksDB.
An LSM-tree keeps key-value pairs and persists them to disk in a Sorted Strings Table (SSTable) with sorted keys; level 0 segments are periodically merged into level 1 by compaction.
B-trees enable faster reads, while LSM-trees enable fast writes.

title: Dense and sparse indexes
article: Database index#Types of indexes > Dense index

definition.text: A dense index has an entry for every record of the table, while a sparse index has entries for only some of the records.

facts.text: A dense index has an index record for every row, each holding the search key and a pointer to the actual record, so records are located directly.
Dense indexes need more write-time maintenance and more memory than sparse ones, but values are found with a binary search and the data need not be ordered.
A sparse index has entries for only some records, such as one per data block, so it needs less maintenance, makes inserts, updates and deletes faster, and uses less memory.
Finding data through a sparse index is slower because a scan across the page typically follows the binary search, and sparse indexes are optional when working with ordered data.

definition.text: A key is a column or group of columns that identifies rows of a table; the main kinds are primary, composite, candidate, foreign, alternate and surrogate keys.

facts.text: A primary key is a column or group of columns that uniquely identifies every row of the table, and a composite key is a primary key made up of multiple columns.
A candidate key is a set of attributes that identifies rows uniquely, a super key is the set of all keys that can uniquely identify the rows, and keys that are not the primary key are alternate keys.
A foreign key is a reference to the primary key of another table.
A surrogate key is a system-generated value that uniquely identifies each entry when no other column could hold the properties of a primary key.

title: Functional dependencies

definition.text: A functional dependency is a relationship between two attributes, typically between the primary key and a non-key attribute of a table.

facts.text: A functional dependency is a relationship between two attributes, typically between the primary key and a non-key attribute within a table.
Second normal form requires that every non-candidate-key attribute depend on the whole candidate key, not just part of it, so the table must have no partial dependency.

A transitive functional dependency occurs when a non-key attribute determines another attribute, such as Author Nationality depending on Author, which depends on Title; third normal form does not permit it.

notes: Singh's wording of partial dependency (S:d7720f4b6eb4, 'primary key determines some other attributes') is loose; the fact uses the Wikipedia 2NF wording (S:036226fc67c1) instead.

title: B-tree

definition.text: A B-tree is a self-balancing tree that keeps data sorted and allows searches, sequential access, insertions and deletions in logarithmic time.

facts.text: A B-tree generalizes the binary search tree by letting nodes have more than two children, which lowers the tree's height and puts the data in fewer separate blocks.
Fewer blocks matter most for trees on disk, which have high latency and large blocks, so B-trees are used in databases and file systems, and they still help in memory because of CPU caches.
In Knuth's definition, a B-tree of order m has at most m children per node, non-root internal nodes have at least m/2 (rounded up), and all leaves are on the same level.
A non-leaf node with k children contains k-1 keys, and these keys act as separation values that divide its subtrees.
Search starts at the root and descends, at each level following the child whose key range contains the search value, usually with binary search inside each node.
Search, insert and delete all take O(log n) time in the worst case, and space is O(n).
Allowing a range of child counts means B-trees rebalance less often than other self-balancing search trees, but they may waste some space because nodes are not entirely full.
The meaning of a B-tree's order varies: Bayer and McCreight define it as the minimum number of keys in a non-root node, while Knuth defines it as the maximum number of children.

notes: Terminology differs between authors (S:ff6759d149c3 is flagged CONTESTED but is a naming ambiguity, not a debate); state each definition by author.

title: B-trees and disk reads
article: B-tree#B-tree usage in databases > Index performance

definition.text: A B-tree index breaks a database into fixed-size pages arranged in levels from a root page down to leaf pages, so a lookup needs only a few disk reads.

facts.text: A B-tree index splits a database into fixed-size pages in levels from a root page to leaf pages that mostly refer to table rows; with more than two children per node, it is shorter than a binary search tree.
Reading a record from disk costs far more than comparing keys because of seek time and rotational delay; at about 10 milliseconds per read, 20 reads to find one record in a million take 0.2 seconds.
An auxiliary index holding the first record of each disk block is about 1% of the size of the original database, and searching it tells which one block of the main database to read.
Indexing the auxiliary index again gives an index of only 100 entries that fits in one disk block, so 3 block reads replace 14 and the record takes 30 milliseconds instead of 150.
This blocking, with disk blocks forming a hierarchy of levels from the root block down to the leaf level, is the core idea behind the B-tree.
Search cost falls from roughly log2 N disk reads to logb N, where b is the blocking factor; with 100 entries per block, log100 1,000,000 is 3 reads.

A B-tree keeps keys sorted, minimizes disk reads with a hierarchical index, uses partially full blocks to speed insertions and deletions, and is the standard index implementation in almost all relational databases.
When an index is searched often, its upper levels may sit in a disk cache and incur no disk read.

title: B+ tree and B* tree

definition.text: The B+ tree and B* tree are variants of the B-tree that keep all record pointers in the leaves or keep nodes more densely packed.

facts.text: A B+ tree can be viewed as a B-tree whose nodes hold only keys, not key-value pairs, with an added bottom level of linked leaves; it consists of a root, internal nodes and leaves, all leaves at the same depth.

Internal nodes hold no record pointers, so every record pointer sits in a leaf; the resulting high fanout, typically 100 or more, makes the tree shallow and cuts the I/O operations needed to find an element.
Search goes from the root to the one leaf that may hold the key, following one branch at each level, so it takes O(log N) where N is the number of keys in the leaves.
Leaves are often linked in a list, which makes range queries and ordered iteration simpler and more efficient; a B-tree cannot build such a list because not all its keys are in the leaves.
Building an index by inserting records one by one is expensive because each starts at the root; bulk-loading instead sorts the data entries by search key first and then builds the tree.
Relational systems such as Db2, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite use B+ trees for table indices, and file systems such as NTFS and XFS use them for metadata indexing.
A 1979 survey says B-trees have become a de facto standard for file organization and discusses their major variations, especially the B+ tree.
A B* tree keeps non-root nodes at least 2/3 full instead of 1/2 and postpones costly node splits by sharing keys with a neighbouring node, a spill that needs no new node.

definition.text: Insertion into a B-tree starts at a leaf and splits full nodes, while deletion removes a key and then rebalances nodes that fall below the minimum size.

facts.text: To insert, search for the leaf node; if it has fewer than the maximum elements, insert the key in order, otherwise split the node into two around a median key.
The median moves up to the parent as a separation value, which may split in turn; a split that reaches the root creates a new root and increases the tree's height.
Deletion has two popular strategies: delete the item and then restructure the tree, or restructure on the way down so the key can be deleted without further restructuring.
A node left below the minimum takes an element from a sibling that can spare one, called a rotation, or else merges with a sibling; merging can continue up to the root.

definition.text: Denormalization is a strategy applied to a previously normalized database to increase performance, by adding redundant copies of data or grouping data.

facts.text: Denormalization improves read performance at the expense of some write performance, by adding redundant copies of data or by grouping data, often to cope with very large numbers of read operations.

In a normalized design a join across several relations stored as separate files can be slow, even prohibitively slow with many relations; once data is sharded or federated, joins across the network add more complexity.
Denormalization has two strategies: the DBMS stores and keeps consistent redundant copies, as with indexed or materialized views, or the designer denormalizes the logical design by hand.

Denormalizing by hand can match the query speed, but the designer must keep the copies consistent with constraints, which slow writes, so under heavy write load it may perform worse than the normalized design.

A denormalized model is not the same as one that was never normalized: denormalization should come only after a satisfactory level of normalization, such as third normal form, with the needed constraints in place.
Typical techniques are storing the count of the many side of a one-to-many relationship in the one side, copying attributes from a relation it joins with, and star schemas.
Advantages are faster retrieval, easier queries and fewer tables; disadvantages are expensive inserts and updates, a more complex design, more redundancy and a greater chance of inconsistent data.
NoSQL databases avoid joins by storing denormalized data, and the extra storage that denormalization needs is a relatively small problem except in truly enormous systems.

definition.text: A log-structured merge-tree (LSM tree) is a data structure that suits indexed access to files with a high insert volume, such as transactional log data.

facts.text: An LSM tree maintains key-value pairs in two or more separate structures, each optimized for its storage medium, and synchronizes data between them efficiently in batches.
In a two-level LSM tree, a smaller component C0 lives entirely in memory and C1 lives on disk; new records go into C0, and when it exceeds a size threshold a contiguous segment is merged into C1.
Its speed comes from writing data sequentially instead of as separate random access requests, which cuts total seek time on hard-disk drives and latency on solid-state drives.
Most real LSM trees have several levels: level 0 sits in main memory and the on-disk data is organized into sorted runs, each sorted by the index key.
A query must search the level 0 tree and also each run, so the system must avoid having too many runs to keep query cost down.
LSM trees were designed for write-intensive workloads; when reads and writes mix, compaction invalidates cached data in buffer caches and reads can see high latency and low throughput.
Cassandra uses an LSM tree index to optimize write throughput, in contrast to the B-tree indexes most databases use.

definition.text: An LSM tree absorbs writes in memory, flushes them to disk as immutable sorted components and later merges those components.

facts.text: A write is first buffered in an in-memory component, often a skip list or B+ tree; when the buffer is full it is flushed sequentially to disk as an immutable sorted component, avoiding costly random writes.
For durability the system may record every incoming write in a write-ahead log before adding it to the memory buffer, so no data is lost if a crash happens during a write.
As data accumulates on disk, a merge process like merge sort consolidates entries across levels; moving level 0 segments into level 1 is called compaction.
Updates are treated as new writes and deletes are marked with a tombstone entry, which is removed later during merging along with obsolete entries.

Levelling keeps one component per level and merges often, giving fewer components but more write amplification; tiering allows several components per level and merges less often, lowering write amplification but raising read costs.

definition.text: A read in an LSM tree checks the in-memory component first and then the disk components from newest to oldest, using Bloom filters to skip components.

facts.text: A point lookup searches the in-memory component first, then disk levels in order, checking newer levels first because they hold the latest updates and deletions, and stops as soon as the key is found.
A Bloom filter per on-disk component is a probabilistic structure that quickly shows a key is definitely absent, so the component can be skipped without reading it.
Point lookup costs O(L) without Bloom filters because each level must be searched, and lookups of existing keys cost O(1) with them.

A range query locates the start in each component, scans sequentially and merges the results in a priority queue to reconcile duplicates, updates and deletes; short ranges cost O(L) and long ranges are dominated by the largest level.

definition.text: The storage engine is the part of the database engine responsible for putting data into permanent storage.

facts.text: The storage engine uses low-level storage structures to serialize the data model so it can be written to the chosen medium, and techniques such as indexing may be used to improve performance.
Data sit in storage in structures that look completely different from the conceptual level, arranged to optimize reconstructing them when users and programs need them.

A DBMS usually reaches storage through the operating system and its file systems, and storage properties and settings are extremely important for efficient operation, so administrators maintain them closely.
Conventional storage is row-oriented, but column-oriented databases also exist.
B-tree is the most widely used indexing structure in almost all relational databases, while LSM-trees are widely used by NoSQL databases such as Cassandra, LevelDB and RocksDB.

definition.text: A hash table is a data structure that implements an associative array, mapping keys to values by using a hash function to compute an index into an array of buckets.

facts.text: During a lookup the key is hashed and the hash says where the value is stored; in a well-dimensioned table the average lookup time does not depend on how many elements it holds.
Search, insert and delete cost Θ(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case, with Θ(n) space; under reasonable assumptions the bounds beat self-balancing binary search trees.
Most designs use an imperfect hash function, so different keys can get the same index; these collisions must be handled, typically by separate chaining or open addressing.
A hash function should spread keys uniformly; a non-uniform distribution increases the number of collisions and the cost of resolving them.
The load factor is the ratio of stored elements to slots and performance deteriorates as it grows, so implementations keep it below a maximum and resize, or rehash, the table when it is reached.

Resizing needs a rehash because items cannot simply be copied to the same indices when the hash function depends on table size; rehashing is simple but expensive, so real-time systems may resize gradually.
Hashing is a space-time tradeoff, and on average hash tables are often more efficient than search trees or any other table lookup structure.

Hash tables implement associative arrays, in-memory tables, caches and sets, and can serve as disk-based database indexes, although B-trees are more popular there; Python dictionaries, Java HashMap and Go maps are built on them.

definition.text: Collision resolution is how a hash table copes with keys that hash to the same index; the two common methods are separate chaining and open addressing.

facts.text: Separate chaining builds a linked list of key-value pairs for each array index; the collided items are chained together and the list is traversed during a lookup.

Open addressing stores every entry in the bucket array and probes from the hashed-to slot, by linear probing, quadratic probing or double hashing, until it finds an empty slot; lookups follow the same sequence.

Open addressing cannot exceed a load factor of 1 and degrades sharply near it, with a maximum of about 0.6 to 0.75; separate chaining degrades gradually, with the best maximum typically between 1 and 3.
Cuckoo hashing and dynamic perfect hashing guarantee O(1) worst-case lookup; cuckoo keeps two tables with separate hash functions and displaces the occupant of a collided slot into the other table.

definition.text: A skip list is a probabilistic data structure that gives O(log n) average search and insertion in an ordered sequence of n elements.

facts.text: Fast search comes from a linked hierarchy of subsequences, each skipping fewer elements than the one above; the bottom layer is an ordinary ordered list and each element appears one layer up with a fixed probability p.

A search starts in the top list and moves right until the current element is greater than or equal to the target, then drops down a level; the expected cost is O(log n), and p trades search cost against storage.

Skip lists have no absolute worst-case guarantee because unlucky coin flips can unbalance them, but they work well in practice and their randomized balancing is argued to be easier to implement; parallel insertions need no global rebalancing.
Redis uses skip lists for ordered sets, RocksDB for its default memtable, and Java for ConcurrentSkipListMap and ConcurrentSkipListSet.

title: Write-ahead log

definition.text: Write-ahead logging is a family of techniques that give a database atomicity and durability: changes are first recorded in an append-only log on stable storage before they are written to the database.

facts.text: Every operation that modifies database state must be logged on disk before the affected pages are modified, which lets the page cache buffer page updates while durability is kept.

After a crash the log is checked to see whether an operation succeeded, partly succeeded or failed, then undone or completed; redo and undo information is usually logged, and a checkpoint applies the logged changes and clears the log.

WAL allows in-place updates, which reduces the need to modify indexes and block lists; shadow paging is the non-in-place alternative for atomic updates, and modern file systems use a WAL variant for metadata, called journaling.

ARIES, a transaction recovery method, applies not only to database systems but to persistent object-oriented languages, recoverable file systems and transaction-based operating systems, and has been implemented in IBM DB2 and other systems.
WAL's central rule is that changes to data files may be written only after the WAL records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage.

Because of that rule, data pages need not be flushed at every commit: after a crash, changes not yet applied to the data pages are redone from the WAL, which is roll-forward recovery, also called REDO.
WAL reduces disk writes: only the sequentially written WAL file must be flushed to commit a transaction, and one fsync of it may commit many concurrent small transactions.
Archiving the WAL supports online backup and point-in-time recovery: restore a prior physical backup and replay the WAL up to the desired time, even if the backup was not an instantaneous snapshot.

title: Inverted index

definition.text: An inverted index is a database index that maps content, such as words, to its locations in a table or in a document or set of documents.

facts.text: Its purpose is fast full-text search, at the cost of more processing when a document is added; it is the most popular data structure in document retrieval systems and a central component of search engines.
A forward index stores the list of words per document; inverting it gives the inverted index, which lists the documents per word.
Without it a query would iterate through every word of every document, which is often not technically realistic; with it, the query jumps to the word by random access.
A record-level inverted index lists the documents for each word; a word-level one also stores each word's positions, which supports phrase searches but needs more processing power and space to build.
PostgreSQL's GIN indexes are inverted indexes with a separate entry for each component value, suited to values that hold several components such as arrays.
Because it lists the documents containing each word, the engine can directly access the documents for each query word to find matches quickly, then rank them by relevance.

A basic inverted index is Boolean: it says whether a word occurs in a document but not how often or where, so it finds matches without ranking them. Frequencies help ranking, and positions support phrase search.

A positional index stores each token's exact positions in its postings list; phrase search fetches the postings of each word, checks the words occur in order, and can use binary search over the postings lists.

definition.text: R-trees are tree data structures for spatial access methods, indexing multi-dimensional information such as geographical coordinates, rectangles or polygons.

facts.text: The key idea is to group nearby objects and represent them by their minimum bounding rectangle one level up; a query that misses a bounding rectangle cannot hit any object inside it.
Like a B-tree, an R-tree is balanced, organizes data in pages and is designed for disk storage; each page holds at most M entries, and best performance has been seen with a minimum fill of 30%-40%.
Search compares each rectangle in a node with the query rectangle and descends only into overlapping children, so most nodes are never read; at the leaves the stored objects are tested precisely.
Real uses include finding all museums within 2 km of a location; nearest-neighbor search keeps a priority queue and expands the nearest entry first; spatial databases typically prefer R-trees.

Insertion descends into the subtree needing least enlargement of its bounding box; a full node is split by a heuristic such as Guttman's quadratic or linear split, and overflows can propagate up to the root, which then grows taller.
The difficulty is a tree that is balanced while its rectangles neither cover much empty space nor overlap much; R-trees give no worst-case guarantee but perform well on real-world data.
The R*-tree reduces overlap with a better subtree choice and splitting heuristic, and avoids some splits by reinserting entries.

Research aims at building an efficient tree from scratch (bulk-loading, for example Sort-Tile-Recursive) and at changing an existing tree; deleting from an underfull page dissolves it and reinserts its children.

definition.text: PostgreSQL provides several index types, B-tree, Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN plus the bloom extension, each using an algorithm suited to different indexable clauses.

facts.text: CREATE INDEX makes a B-tree by default, which fits the most common situations; other types are chosen with the USING keyword.

B-trees handle equality and range queries on sortable data, can return rows in sorted order, and serve prefix patterns such as LIKE 'foo%' but not LIKE '%bar'; Hash indexes store a 32-bit hash code and handle only equality.

GiST and SP-GiST are infrastructures for many indexing strategies: GiST covers geometric types and nearest-neighbor searches, SP-GiST supports non-balanced structures such as quadtrees, k-d trees and tries.

GIN indexes are inverted indexes for values with several components, such as arrays; BRIN indexes store minimum and maximum summaries of consecutive block ranges, so they work best when column values correlate with the physical row order.
